### 2026-11-13 — PLANNER-A — DECISION — unblocked: the sidecar-removal test's own delete is bounded and retried (option 1); AGENTS.md's HANDOFF still to commit; go on with 4b

**The diagnosis holds** (read `tests/cross_process.rs:897-906`,
`shared/sidecar.rs:201` and `shared/lock.rs:247`). The panic is the test's
own `remove_dir_all(&gone)`, not an assertion. A child keeps its descriptor
on the moved directory and, as built in 2c, goes on creating
`intent.lock` and `lock-info`'s temp name there (`openat` with `O_CREAT`)
until an open fails. Only then does it reopen by path. A name created between
`remove_dir_all`'s listing and its `rmdir` gives ENOTEMPTY. That's expected
engine behaviour and the test's own race, so it isn't an engine bug. The
comment's "can't race" is wrong.

**DECISION: option 1,** not option 3.
- **Why:** removing the directory at any moment, mid-call included, is the
  real case (`git clean -fdx` doesn't wait for a pause), and today's test
  shows the engine takes it with no unexpected error and no lost write.
  Option 3 would drop that mid-call coverage to avoid a retry of a
  filesystem action the test itself performs.
- **The rule, clarified:** "no retries inside tests" is about assertions and
  engine calls; it stays absolute there. A test may retry **its own
  environment action** (here, deleting a directory that a live child is
  legitimately writing into) when the retry is bounded, the race is named in
  a comment, and exhausting the bound fails the test.
- **The change:** `remove_dir_all(&gone)` in a loop that retries only on
  `DirectoryNotEmpty` (and `NotFound` counts as done), at most 50 tries,
  10 ms apart, then `panic!` with the error. Fix the comment to say what
  races and why the retry is safe. The assertions stay as they are.
- **Undo check:** none needed (no fix to undo); run the test alone 50 times
  locally under `MNEMO_STRESS=1` and give the count in the DONE.
- **Where:** its own `test(shared): …` commit in 4b's PR. No separate PR.

**Missed HANDOFF:** my 2026-11-13 tmux entry ("the team moves to tmux…")
lists `AGENTS.md` (the "Running in tmux…" subsection) for the next
coordination sync. `b8f6297` synced PLAN.md only, and AGENTS.md is still
uncommitted. Commit `AGENTS.md` alone with the message

opens, with the command as the note; `compact_file_waiting`; `serve --mcp

**Fix before merging** (one new commit each, or together; then squash):
1. **Embedding before the lock** (the note's protocol step 1, "slow work
   first, unlocked"; 4a's Python already does it). The DONE lists this as a
   limitation for later. I don't accept that for v0.14. A local
   `--embed-cmd` can take hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, and under
   `--shared` every other session waits behind it, up to its 10 s deadline
   (a hook's 2 s).
   - **MCP, shared mode:** the four text sites (`remember`, `recall`,
     `cache_put_semantic`, `cache_get_semantic`; `embed_text_via_server`).
     In `shared_tools_call`, when the tool takes `text` and the server has an
     embedder, embed it **before** the window through
     `SharedMnemo::embedder_arc`, and hand the vector to the tool (for
     example an `Option<Vec<f32>>` that `embed_text_via_server` returns
     first), so no tool is restructured. The text still goes to the tool
     wherever it's stored or used for the model name, and the error messages
     stay the same. The plain server may stay as it is (it holds the file
     for its life anyway).
   - **The CLI:** `remember`, `update` and `thread ingest` with
     `--embed-cmd` currently `open_w` first, then embed (thread ingest
     embeds every turn under the lock). Embed first, then take the write
     window. The file's dimensions are needed for the identity: prefer
     getting them without a second KDF (if the header or a plaintext field
     has them); otherwise a waiting read-only open to read them, closed
     before the embedder runs, is acceptable (one KDF, about 15 to 45 ms).
     A vector whose length doesn't match the file is refused after the open
     with the same error as today, writing nothing.
   - **Tests:** a shared MCP server whose `--embed-cmd` sleeps (say 1.5 s):
     during its `remember` with `text`, a CLI write with `--wait 500ms`
     succeeds. The same for the CLI's `remember --embed-cmd` against a
     shared reader or writer. Check both against the old order (undo).
2. **A tracked CLI `recall` can wait twice its deadline.** On `Locked`
   after `open_rw`'s full wait, the fallback `open_ro` waits a full
   deadline again (up to 20 s by default). An exclusive holder that kept the
   write out keeps the read out too, so the second wait almost never helps.
   Make the fallback one try (`Mnemo::open_read_only` /
   `_with_key`). One line in the CLI test or a comment saying why.

**Noted, no change:** an unknown MCP tool name goes to a write window; since
RB-007.6 a window that seals nothing commits nothing, so it costs only the
lock.

    the header through a new `Mnemo::peek_dimensions(path)` (page 0, no
    key, no lock, no KDF). They start the embedder and embed, then take the
    write lock (`open_w`), then `set_embedder` (the identity check) and
    write.
  - `update` keeps `update_text`'s width check, with the same
    `DimensionMismatch`.
  - A header that can't be read (torn) falls back to the old order. (A
    write open heals it.)
  - `thread ingest` plans under a short waiting read
    (`ingest_thread_texts`, one KDF, closed before the embedder runs),
    embeds, then takes the write lock and plans again. If the plan is the
    same it writes with `ingest_thread_with_vectors`. If another process
    ingested meanwhile, it embeds under the lock only the texts it doesn't
    have yet.
- **`recall`'s read-only fallback** after `Locked` is now one try
  (`Mnemo::open_read_only` / `_with_key`), with a comment saying why.
- **Tests** (`cli_shared.rs`, 2 new; both sync on a marker file the slow
  embedder writes when a request arrives, not on sleeps):
  - a shared MCP server with a 1.5 s embedder: during its `remember` with
    `text`, `mnemo --wait 500ms import` succeeds;
  - the CLI's `remember --embed-cmd` with a 1.5 s embedder: a shared write
    with a 500 ms deadline succeeds meanwhile.
- **Undo checks, both caught:** MCP without `pre_embed`; the CLI forced
  into the old order.
  - The first version of the CLI test synced on a 500 ms sleep and passed
    with the old order. A freshly built binary's first launch on macOS can
    take longer than that, so the write got in before the CLI started. The
    marker fixed it.

**Runs on `8bdf795`:** CI 43501371709, **13 of 14 green; `rust

```

```
That test passed on Windows on every earlier run (PR 68's three heads, PR
69, PR 70's first two heads).

**My diagnosis: the test harness misreports an allowed error, not an engine
bug.**
- The kill test allows `Locked` and asserts only that nothing else fails.
- `role_writer` treats `Locked` as "try again", but its first call,
  `open_child`, loops on `Locked` only while the stop file is absent
  (`Err(MnemoError::Locked { .. }) if !stopped() => continue`), and
  returns any other case as an error.
- Writer `w1g4`, restarted after its fourth kill near the end of the 6 s
  run, was opening when the parent created the stop file. Its open waited
  its 2 s deadline (slower Windows runners, a compaction or another writer
  holding the file) and got `Locked`. With the stop file there, that was
  reported as an error and the process exited 3.
- No acknowledged write was missing, nothing was stored twice, and
  `verify` wasn't reached: the run failed on the child's exit code first.
- It's in no file 4b changed. The children's `open_shared` and the lock
  layer aren't touched by fix round 1.

**Why I stopped:** your step 3 rule, "an intermittent failure is a bug until
shown otherwise; if one turns up, stop and log it." The fix is a change to a
merged test's harness.

**Proposed fix** (one line in the harness, not applied): in `open_child`,
`Locked` once the stop file exists means "stop": return a value the roles
treat as a clean exit (code 0), because `Locked` is the allowed error and a
child that was told to stop has nothing left to do. Everything else stays as
it is.
- No retry is added: the open already loops on `Locked` while the run lasts.
- It removes only the misreport of the allowed error at shutdown.
- I'd also check the other roles' first calls for the same shape
  (`role_reader` uses `open_child` too).

**What I think happened (not proven):** the 300 ms is a timing bound on
live processes.
- A child makes the directory again only at its next lock-file open after
  the deletion. That's a call after its stale descriptor stops working.
- The bounded delete retry added in 4b can itself take up to about 500 ms
  while the children write into the moved directory.
- On a loaded runner, with this binary's other cross-process tests running
  their own children at the same time, two children may not each finish a
  call inside 300 ms.
- I can't rule out an engine path where a child keeps a stale sidecar
  longer, though I found none by reading:
  - every failed lock-file open reopens by path once per call;
  - an `Unavailable` keeps the old `Arc` and tries again on the next call.

**Why I stopped:** the step 3 rule (an intermittent failure is a bug until
shown otherwise), and this is an assertion, which your last decision kept
absolute.

**Options**, none applied:
1. **A bounded wait instead of the fixed sleep.** Poll `side.is_dir()` up
   to, say, 10 s, then assert. It's the same claim ("the children make it
   again") with a deadline that fits a loaded runner. This changes the
   assertion's timing, not what it asserts.
2. **Make the children's next call deterministic:** a marker each writer
   child writes after every acknowledged write; wait for one new marker per
   child after the last removal, then assert. No timing guess at all.
3. **Run the test alone** (a separate test binary or `--test-threads=1` for
   that file), to cut the load, and keep the 300 ms. This doesn't fix the
   bound, only the load.

### 2026-11-13 — PLANNER-A — DECISION — unblocked: the sidecar test waits for calls, not a fixed 300 ms (option 2, two acknowledged writes per child, 10 s cap)

**Read:** `tests/cross_process.rs` at `origin/rel0140-rekey2` (the fixed
`sleep(300ms)` then `assert!(side.is_dir())`) and `shared/lock.rs:241-253`
(a failed `lock_file(INTENT)` reopens the sidecar by path once per call).
The assertion claims "the children make it again at their next calls", but
it checks that with a wall-clock guess. On a loaded runner, a 300 ms window
can hold no call that started after the last removal. The diagnosis fits.
No engine path that keeps a stale sidecar across a call was found, by the
Worker or by me.

**DECISION: option 2,** with one refinement:
- After the last removal, wait until **each** writer child has acknowledged
  **two** more writes. The first may come from a call that started before
  the removal; the second's call started after the first's acknowledgement,
  so it started after the removal. Then assert `side.is_dir()`.
- Cap the wait at 10 s. Hitting the cap fails the test with the counts, so
  a child that stops making progress is still caught.

### 2026-11-13 — PLANNER-A — DECISION — step 5's stop: fix reader starvation in v0.14 (readers keep the intent lock while a writer commits); writers' p99 measured again after; the refused-write reload stays; the backoff stays

**The numbers are good where it matters most:** 0.05 ms per call when
nobody wrote, no-op windows free (RB-007.6 holds), about 20 commits a
second, 1.6 to 17.8 MB per handle. **The stop is real.**

**Why readers starve** (read `shared/lock.rs:163-219`):
- A writer drops the intent lock as soon as it gets the main lock
  (line 180), so the intent lock is free while it commits.
- A reader that comes in then gets the intent lock, finds the main lock
  held, and lets the intent lock go (the one-try rule, RB-006.4 rec. 1).
- The next writer takes the intent lock exclusively and waits on the main
  lock, so with two or more writers some writer always holds the intent
  lock, and readers never get in.
- With one writer writing back to back, its next call finds both locks free
  microseconds after its commit, and wins.

The one-try rule was there so busy readers couldn't starve a writer. As
written, it starves readers.

**DECISION 1: fix it in v0.14** (step 5b, in step 5's PR). v0.14's claim is
several processes on one brain. A script writing a batch in shared mode
(DOGFOOD-1's `--from-file` does exactly that) would keep a hook's 2 s read
out for the whole batch. REVIEWER-B reviews the lock layer at READY anyway.

**The rule, refining RB-006.4 rec. 1:**
- A reader takes the intent lock shared and tries the main lock once.
- **If the main lock is free or held shared,** it gets in, or it lets the
  intent lock go at once: today's rule, so busy readers still can't starve
  a writer.
- **If the main lock is held exclusively** (a shared `try_lock` fails only
  then), the reader **keeps** the intent lock shared while it waits for
  that writer, within its deadline and cancel. The next writer then can't
  take the intent lock and queues behind the waiting readers. When the
  writer's commit ends, the readers get in together, and then the next
  writer goes.
- That alternates a writer with a batch of readers (phase-fair), and needs
  no new lock file and no format change.
- Every lock still goes through `LockedFile`, and a cancel or the deadline
  drops both locks (the existing tests must still hold).
- Update the note's "Writer preference" section and the throughput
  paragraph, marked "(since step 5)".

**Then measure again** (cells 5, 6 and 8 at 10K and 100K; **three runs
each** for the multi-process cells, given the busy daemons, with the median
run reported):
- **Readers:** 1 writer back to back with 1 reader: at least 10 reads a
  second and a read-wait p99 under 200 ms. 4 writers with 2 readers, and 8
  with 2: a read-wait p99 under 500 ms.
- **No regression:** the 8-readers-against-a-writer test still passes, and
  commits a second fall by no more than 10 %.
- **Writers:** if 8 writers' p99 at 10K is still over 500 ms, try one
  addition: **a newcomer defers to an older waiter.** A caller that has
  waited longer than the young period (15 ms) holds a `waiting.lock` in the
  sidecar shared; a caller just starting finds it held (an exclusive
  `try_lock` fails) and backs off once before trying the intent lock.
  That stops a writer's next call from barging past writers that have
  waited. Keep it only if it brings the p99 under 500 ms without breaking
  the reader targets. If neither does, report the numbers and stop: then
  it's a v0.14 scope question for the user.
- **Cell 8:** opens complete within their deadline. Report p50 and p99 with
  each compaction's duration, since an open during a compaction rightly
  waits for it. Then the Windows one-off.
- **Tests:** in `tests/shared_lock.rs`, a reader against a writer looping
  back to back must finish at least 20 reads in 2 s, and, for the newcomer
  rule if it's kept, 4 writers each committing within a bound. Check each
  against its change undone. A cross-process version in `cross_process.rs`
  if it's cheap.

**DECISION 2: the refused-write reload stays** ((b), not adopted). Clearing
the stamp at every write window's start is RB-006.1's rule. Proving that "the
closure failed before changing anything" covers all of the handle's
in-memory state is a new correctness argument, for about 32 ms at 100K after
a validation error, which is rare. Step 6's incremental catch-up makes that
reload cheap anyway; note it there.

**DECISION 3: the backoff stays,** by the rule. Keep the dev-hooks switch.
Re-run cell 7 once after the fairness change and apply the same rule.

**Also noted for step 6:** a shared write costs about 9 ms more than a plain
one (5 fsyncs against 3, the lease). Whether the lease can share the
commit's syncs without weakening RB-006.11 (a) is a question for step 6's
design, not now.

**This counts as fix round 1 for step 5.** Log DONE when the PR is green
(the bench, the JSON with both runs labelled, the note's numbers, the
fairness change and its tests), and stop before merging.

### 2026-11-13 — PLANNER-A — NEEDS-USER — v0.14 scope: which lock fairness ships (step 5's second stop)

**The question for the user:** the first fix made readers fair but slowed
writers sharply against back-to-back readers, and 8 writers' slowest 1 %
stays about 2.5 s. Only a real queue fixes both, and that's a design change.

**The options** (from the Worker's BLOCKED entry, with my read):
1. **Ship today's rule** and document it. A continuous writer (a batch in
   shared mode) locks readers out: they wait the full deadline and fail with

   slows to under 1 commit a second (p99 2.9 s at 10K, 5.5 s at 100K), but

   sidecar): a new design, a REVIEWER-B pass on paper, then code. Probably a

  3. then the commit's pre-write check, `Mnemo::ensure_not_replaced`
     (`store/load.rs`, step 1's "a handle refuses to write to a replaced
     file"), refuses with `Replaced`.
  
  Nothing was written and nothing acknowledged, so **no write is lost:
  the outcome is safe.** But:
  - the test's writer allows only `ReplacedDuringWrite` (the rename after
    the commit), not this earlier window;
  - the shared surface returns a plain-handle error whose advice ("Reopen
    it") doesn't apply: a shared handle's next call reloads anyway;
  - `docs/shared-mode.md`'s error table doesn't list `Replaced`.
- **Not caused by step 5:** that case has 3 writers and no readers, and the
  change touches only readers. It's a timing race in step 3's test. It ran
  green on every push and PR since step 3, and 4 of 4 times locally
  (0.13.2 binary from my scratchpad; 0 replaced each time, 57 to 71
  compactions a run).
- **Options:**
  1. Engine: inside a shared write window, map `Replaced` from the commit's
     pre-write check to `ReplacedDuringWrite`. Both mean "not in the file
     at the path", and shared callers then see the one error the docs list.
     Test: a failpoint that renames over the path between the window's
     identity check and the commit, which fails without the mapping.
  2. Test only: the writer child also allows `Replaced` under
     `XP_ALLOW_REPLACED` (counted, never acknowledged), and the docs'
     error table lists `Replaced` for shared mode.

  My read: option 1. It's small, keeps the shared error surface as
  documented, and fixes the advice.

### 2026-11-13 — PLANNER-A — DECISION — unblocked: the writer test's bound becomes 5 s (LOCK-2 restores 1 s); a pre-commit `Replaced` in a shared window stays its own error, with the right advice

**1. `a_writer_gets_in_against_eight_busy_readers`: option 2, a 5 s bound.**
- The 1 s bound was the note's spec under the old rule. Readers-first
  (the user's decision) raised this test's worst wait from about 11 ms to
  200–325 ms locally, and a CI runner crossed 1 s. That's the accepted cost,
  not a new bug.
- Option 1 (only "within the 10 s deadline") would barely test anything: it
  catches only total starvation. A 5 s bound still catches a real
  regression, and it's about 15 times the local worst.
- Assert every write gets in with no `Locked`, and the worst wait under
  5 s, and print the worst and the median, so a later run shows the trend.
- Update the note's test line ("under 5 s since step 5; LOCK-2 restores a
  tight bound"), and add "restore this test's 1 s bound" to LOCK-2's entry
  in my option 2 decision's carried list (in your DONE; I keep the list).

**2. The 0.13.2 compactor's `Replaced`: neither option as written.**
- `Replaced` before the commit means **nothing was written**. Retrying the
  call is safe. `ReplacedDuringWrite` means the write may be in the old,
  replaced file. Mapping one onto the other (option 1) would tell callers a
  safe case is the unsafe one. Keep them apart.
- **What to change:**
  - In a shared window, the pre-commit `Replaced` keeps its variant, but
    its message for a shared handle says what's true there: "the file at
    … was replaced (an older build's compaction) before this write;
    nothing was written, and the next call follows the new file". No
    "Reopen it" for a shared handle. The plain handle's message stays.
  - The window clears the stamp on it, as for any failed write, so the
    next call reloads. Confirm that's already so.
  - `docs/shared-mode.md`'s error table gains `Replaced` (Python:
    `MnemoError`, or its own class if one exists), "nothing was written;
    call again".
  - The test's writer child accepts `Replaced` (counted, never
    acknowledged) alongside `ReplacedDuringWrite`, and the job prints both
    counts. The "no acknowledged write lost" assertion is unchanged.
  - **A test, if a hook makes it cheap:** a rename over the path between
    the window's identity check and the commit gives `Replaced`, with the
    new message, and the next call sees the new file. If it needs a new
    failpoint, add one (failpoints builds only).
- It only happens with a pre-0.14 binary renaming without its lock: the
  named mixed-version exception, which the upgrade note covers.

#### RB-006 (REVIEWER-B, 2026-11-13) — the 12.4 shared-access design note, and one finding in shipped code

Reviewed: `docs/design/12.4-shared-access.md` at `9fc260b`, against the engine on `main` at `233eba4` (v0.13.2). The rest of the batch is in `reviewer_notes.md`.

- **`RB-006.10` is about shipped code** (v0.13.2 and earlier). It needs someone else to be able to create a name in the brain's directory. Step 1's commit (`35ab403`, not released) already makes it impractical.
- **`RB-006.11` and `RB-006.12` are about a design.** No code exists, so nothing can be attacked today. They're here because the brief says security findings go only in this file, and because two of them describe how to break a property the engine documents.

##### RB-006.10 — [SECURITY] [LOW] Compaction and export write through a symlink planted at their fixed temp name

- **Status:** `ACCEPTED`
- **Where:** `mnemo/src/store/maintenance.rs:724-746` (`{path}.compact-tmp`, created by `create_secret` → `open_with_lock(.., create = true)`, `load.rs:22-25`: create and truncate, following symlinks) and `maintenance.rs:65-75` with `load.rs:76-80` (`{dest}.export-tmp`, the same options).
- **Tested** at `233eba4` (`rb6/tests/tmp_name.rs`), with a symlink at the temp name pointing at another file the same user owns:

| Call | Result | The other file | The path afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Mnemo::compact_file(brain)` | `Ok` | overwritten: 122,880 bytes starting `MNEM` (the compacted brain) | the brain's path is now **a symlink to the other file**; it still opens, with 3 memories |
| `export_encrypted(dest)` | `Ok` | overwritten the same way | `dest` is now a symlink to the other file |

- **What it takes.** Someone who can create a name in the brain's directory (or the export's), and can't already do worse:
  - another local user, where the brain is in a sticky or shared directory (they can create names there but can't touch the user's files);
  - a repository that carries a symlink at `<brain>.compact-tmp`, for a project that keeps its brain at a path inside the working tree. A default brain under the common git directory isn't reachable that way.

  The victim then runs `mnemo compact`, `mnemo rekey --rotate` or an export. The attacker picks which of the victim's files is destroyed. They don't control what's written (it's the brain's header and ciphertext). The brain's path ends up as a symlink, so later writes to the brain go to that file too.
- **Step 1 (`35ab403`), by reading only, not tested:** the temp name becomes `<dest>.<what>-<pid>-<n>-<nanoseconds>.tmp`, which an attacker can't predict in practice. It's still opened with `create(true)` and no exclusive flag, and `is_file_at` follows a symlink at the path, so a correctly guessed name would still be written through.
- **Recommendation:**
  1. Create both temp files with `create_new(true)` (`O_EXCL`), which refuses any existing name, a symlink included. With step 1's unique names a collision is then an error to retry under a new name, never a write through someone else's file.
  2. Add the test: a symlink at the temp name (for the old fixed name, and for whatever name the code is about to use, by making the name generator injectable in the test) leaves its target byte-identical.
  3. 12.4 adds fixed names next to the brain (`X.mnemo-shared/`, `intent.lock`, `lock-info`). `RB-006.11` (b) is the same issue for those.
- **Would I hold anything for it?** No release. It belongs in step 1's PR, which is open on these lines now.
- **Planner Triage:** `ACCEPTED` (PLANNER-A, 2026-11-13), **in v0.14.0 step 1's PR**, which is open on these lines: both temp files (compaction and export) are created with `create_new(true)` (`O_EXCL`), a collision retries under a new name, and a test plants a symlink at the temp name and asserts the other file is untouched and the call fails or retries cleanly. Neutral commit message. Move into PLAN.md after v0.14.0 ships.

##### RB-006.11 — [SECURITY] [MEDIUM] The lock layer's design: the generation lease assumes one writer session at a time; the sidecar directory is trusted by name; a shared handle keeps its secret

- **Status:** `ACCEPTED`

###### (a) The generation lease is taken once per handle, and its argument needs sessions that don't interleave

- **The code** (`mnemo/src/store/records.rs:1292-1314`). A v9 page's generation is the id of the transaction that writes it, `wal_seq + 1` (`records.rs:533-539`). Before a handle seals its first page it commits a header-only transaction that raises `wal_seq` (`ensure_gen_lease`), then sets `gen_leased` for the rest of the handle's life (`:1312`). The comment gives the reason: a session that crashes before committing leaves pages (orphan data pages, or uncommitted WAL frames) sealed under an id "the next session would hand out again, for the same pages (allocation is deterministic). An attacker holding a copy of the crashed file could then swap an orphan back in under a matching generation." Burning one id per session makes "every id this session uses … above every id any earlier session used".
- **Why it stops holding in shared mode.** "Earlier session" assumes one session ends before the next begins, which the lifetime lock guarantees today. Shared handles interleave:
  1. Handles C and P are both long-lived and both took their lease long ago.
  2. P takes the exclusive lock at `wal_seq = M`, writes its data pages straight to their home pages under generation `M + 1` (`flush.rs:240`, before the WAL commit at `:568`), and dies, or gets an I/O error (`RB-006.1`). The header still says `M`.
  3. C's next write catches up to `M`. Its `gen_leased` is already true, so it takes no lease. It allocates the same pages (same free list, same `next_page`) and seals different contents under `(page, M + 1)`, and commits.
  4. Anyone with a copy of the file from step 2 and write access to the file can put P's page back. Its tag is valid for `(page, M + 1)`, which is what C's catalog row expects.
- **Impact.** The rollback protection v9's page AAD exists for (`pager.rs:233-245`) no longer covers pages written by a writer that failed before its commit. The attacker needs a copy of the file taken at the right moment and write access to it (a synced folder, a backup, a shared disk), and what they can restore is a record a legitimate writer sealed but never committed, in place of the one that was. It's narrow. It's also exactly the case the engine's own comment says it rules out.
- **Not in the note.** The crash table's row "a writer, before its WAL commit: nothing was committed; the stamp check sees no change" is true and is the problem: nothing tells the next writer.
- **Recommendation:** one of these, decided before step 2:
  1. **Take the lease in every exclusive write window** (reset `gen_leased` when the lock is released). It costs one header-only commit per write: two more fsyncs (`flush.rs:107-115`), so a write goes from 3 fsyncs to 5. Not timed. The note's "about 16 ms" and its commit rate change with it.
  2. Skip the lease when the handle can prove nobody else held the exclusive lock since its own last commit. I don't see how it can: a writer that fails before its commit leaves no trace, which is the point. If a cheap durable mark exists (a byte outside page 0 written before the first data page), it's the same cost as the lease.
  3. Put something per-writer into the generation (a format change, through the format-version policy).
  4. Accept it and write it down in the threat model, with the narrowing above.
- I'd take 1 for the first version and measure it in step 5's bench.

###### (b) The sidecar directory is trusted because of its name

- **The design.** `X.mnemo-shared/` is created 0700 next to the brain if missing, and holds `intent.lock`, `lock-info` and `presence/*.lock`. The note says "a running handle recreates what it needs".
- **Finding.** Where someone else can create names in the brain's directory (the two cases in `RB-006.10`), they can be there first:
  1. **As a directory they own.** They hold `intent.lock` exclusively and every shared call on the brain waits its full deadline and fails. They hold or remove presence files, so agents look alive or dead as they choose; with "a dead holder's claim lapses at once" that releases other agents' claims.
  2. **As a symlink**, or with a symlink inside it. The engine then creates its lock files wherever the link points, and writes the `lock-info` line (the operation, pid, start time and tool) into whatever `lock-info` names. Opened with create-and-truncate, that overwrites a file of the attacker's choosing, as in `RB-006.10`, but on every long operation rather than only on a compaction.
- **Recommendation**, for step 2's code:
  1. Create the directory with `mkdir` (never "create if missing, else use"), and on finding one, check with `lstat` that it's a real directory owned by the caller with no group or other access. If it isn't, don't use it: take the main lock alone and say so once.
  2. Open every file in it with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and create with `O_EXCL` where the file is new. Open relative to the directory's descriptor (`openat`) so the check and the use are the same directory.
  3. Write `lock-info` to a new exclusive temp name and rename it into place, or make it a file that's only ever appended to and never truncated.
  4. Tests for each: a foreign-owned directory, a symlinked directory, and a symlink at each fixed name.

###### (c) A shared handle keeps its secret for its whole life

- **The design.** A shared handle keeps "its secret (zeroized on drop), the unwrapped data key, and the KDF parameters". Today's handle keeps the data key and drops the secret once the file is open (the `Mnemo` struct has no field for it, `store/mod.rs`).
- **Finding.** This is needed: every compaction makes a new data key (`RB-006.2`), so without the secret every `mnemo compact` would end every session. But it's a change in what a long-lived process holds, and the note states it without marking it. A passphrase is worth more to an attacker than a data key: it survives a rotation, and people reuse them. It now sits in an MCP server's memory for hours.
- **Recommendation:**
  1. Say it in the note's trust-boundary text and in the docs.
  2. Prefer fetching the secret again when it's needed (from the keychain once 12.3 ships, or from whatever supplied it) over keeping it. Keep it only where there's nothing to ask.
  3. For a raw-key file the kept secret is the key itself, which changes nothing.

- **Would I want it settled before step 2's code?** (a) and (b), yes. (c) is a sentence now and a choice at 12.3.
- **Planner Triage:** `ACCEPTED` (PLANNER-A, 2026-11-13).
  - **(a), before step 2:** recommendation 1. The lease is taken in every exclusive write window (`gen_leased` resets when the lock is released). Measure the cost in step 5's bench (3 to 5 fsyncs a write) and correct the note's numbers. If step 5 finds it too slow, recommendation 2 (a cheaper durable mark) is the place to look, with a written argument, not 4.
  - **(b), before step 2:** all four recommendations: `mkdir` and an `lstat` ownership-and-mode check; `O_NOFOLLOW` and `openat` relative to the directory; `lock-info` written by temp name and rename; the three tests.
  - **(c):** now, a sentence in the note's trust-boundary text and in the docs. At 12.3, prefer fetching the secret again from the keychain over keeping it.
  - These stay here until v0.14.0 ships.

| (b) rec. 4 | The three tests | `tests/shared_lock.rs`: the symlinked directory, the directory open to others, a symlink at each fixed name | They pass. A directory owned by another user isn't tested (it needs a second user), as the Worker's DONE says |

**What I'd still note about (b), none of it a hole:**
- **A handle keeps the directory's descriptor for its whole life.** If the directory is deleted and made again, the old handle uses neither (RB-007.7 in `reviewer_notes.md`). It loses writer preference; it never follows a name it didn't check.
- **Whoever can make the sidecar unusable turns writer preference off for that brain** (create it first as their own directory, or as a symlink). The handle then takes the main lock alone and says so in `notices()`, which nothing prints yet. They gain nothing unless they can also open the brain to hold its lock, which is `RB-007.9`.
- **A umask that clears owner bits** (0277, say) makes a directory the checks accept and nothing can be created in. Each call then silently skips the intent lock. Check after `mkdir` that the mode is exactly 0700, and `fchmod` it if not.
- **Windows:** no owner or mode check, as documented. A junction or a symlink is refused; a directory another user made in a shared folder is used.

##### RB-007.9 — [SECURITY] [LOW] A brain is created with the process's umask, so on most machines other local users can read the file and can hold its lock

- **Status:** `VERIFIED` (RB-008, `a3c0aae` on release-0.14.0, before the tag)
- **Where:** `open_and_lock_once` (`mnemo/src/store/load.rs`): `OpenOptions` with `create` or `create_new` and no mode, for `Mnemo::create` and for compaction's new file. Every version.
- **Tested** at `19edf8b` (`rb7/tests/inplace.rs`): a new brain has mode **0644** under the usual umask 022. The inspector's page file and the git export already ask for 0600 (`bin/mnemo/inspect.rs:896`, `bin/mnemo/export.rs:125`), and shared mode's sidecar is 0700; the brain itself is the one left open.
- **What another local user gets**, where they can reach the path (a home directory that is 0755, a shared project folder, `/tmp`). By reading; I have no second user to run it as:
  1. **The ciphertext and the header**, to copy. Page 0 holds the salt, the KDF parameters and the wrapped data key in the clear, so a copy is enough to guess a passphrase offline, at Argon2id's cost per guess. A raw-key file gives nothing to guess.
  2. **The lock.** `flock` needs only an open descriptor, and a read-only one will do. Holding it shared blocks every writer; holding it exclusive blocks everyone. Each shared call then waits its deadline and fails with `Locked`, with no holder named.
  3. In shared mode, the 0700 sidecar keeps them out of the intent lock, and (2) makes that beside the point.
- **Impact:** low. The contents stay encrypted, and it needs a local account and a reachable path. It matters more for 12.x's team and project brains, which live in directories people share on purpose, and where a group-readable brain may even be wanted.
- **Recommendation:**
  1. Create brains (and compaction's replacement, which should keep the old file's mode and owner rather than reset it) with mode 0600 on Unix.
  2. Leave an existing file's mode alone, so a brain someone made group-readable on purpose stays that way; `compact` copies the mode across.
  3. A line in the README's security section: file permissions are the user's, and 0600 is the default from v0.14.
  4. A test for the created mode and for compaction keeping a mode.
- **Would I hold step 3 for it?** No.
- **Planner Triage:** `ACCEPTED` (PLANNER-A, 2026-11-13), **step 2c**, all four: new brains and compaction's new file are created 0600 on Unix; compaction (and `rekey --rotate`) gives the new file the old file's mode, so a brain made group-readable on purpose stays so; an existing file's mode is never changed; tests for both. The README line goes in at the v0.14.0 release (PLANNER-A HANDOFF). Neutral commit and PR wording ("create new brain files owner-only; compaction keeps the mode"). **Also from the RB-006.11 (b) notes above, step 2c:** after `mkdir`, check the sidecar's mode is exactly 0700 and `fchmod` it if a umask cleared owner bits.

- **Worker, 2026-11-13 (step 2c, PR 67, `36814e9`):** RB-007.9 and the sidecar mode are done as triaged.
  - A new brain, a compaction's new file and an export's temp file are opened with mode 0600 on Unix (`owner_only` in `store/load.rs`, applied only when the file is created).
  - Compaction then gives its new file the old file's permissions (`copy_mode`, an fchmod through the open handle), so `rekey --rotate` keeps the mode too.
  - `Mnemo::create` over an existing file leaves its mode alone.
  - After its checks, the sidecar directory is given 0700 with `fchmod` when its owner bits aren't all set.
  - Tests in `tests/shared_fixes.rs`: a new brain is 0600; a 0640 brain stays 0640 through a compaction; an export is 0600; an existing 0644 file is unchanged by `create`; a 0500 sidecar becomes 0700 and is used. Each fails with its fix undone.
  - Not done: the owner isn't copied (it needs privileges), and Windows is unchanged.

|---|---|---|
| New brains, compaction's new file and exports created 0600 | `owner_only` sets mode 0600 on every creating open (`store/load.rs`, `open_and_lock_once`; the export temp in `store/maintenance.rs`) | Tested: a new brain is 0600 under umask 022 (0644 at `19edf8b`) |
| Compaction keeps the old file's mode; an existing file's mode is never changed | `copy_mode` right after the temp file is created (`compact_file_secret`) | Tested: a 0644 brain is 0644 after a compaction. The Worker's tests cover 0640 and an export |

| The README line | Not yet: it's in the release HANDOFF | |

**One line the release text should carry.** Every brain made before v0.14 is 0644 under the usual umask, and nothing in v0.14 changes that: compaction keeps the old mode by design. So the exposure RB-007.9 describes stays for every existing brain until its owner runs `chmod 600` on it. The README's security line and the CHANGELOG entry say new files are owner-only; add that existing brains keep their mode and how to tighten one. This isn't a new finding, only the part of RB-007.9 that the code change can't reach.

##### Also checked in this pass, nothing found

- **`remove_dead_compaction_temps`** (`store/maintenance.rs`). It removes only regular files in the brain's own directory, owned by this user, named exactly `<brain>.compact-<pid>-<n>-<8 hex>.tmp`, whose pid isn't this process and isn't running, and only while the brain's exclusive lock is held. Tested: a dead compaction's temp went; this process's own temp, five look-alike names (a `.bak` suffix, the old fixed `.compact-tmp`, a nine-digit hex field, another brain's prefix, an export temp) and a symlink carrying a temp's name all stayed, and the symlink's target was untouched.
- **Recovery with the held data key** (`store/open.rs`, `sealed_under`, `load_locked_with`). A pending WAL or a torn-header candidate is accepted without the KDF only when the header it leads to is v9 and its seal verifies under the key the handle already holds. A header sealed under that key was written by someone who had it, so this gives the handle nothing it didn't have. Anything else still goes through the secret.
- **The `lock-info` note from plain long operations** (`lock_exclusive`, `Held::announce`). The operation name comes from the caller, has control characters removed and is cut at 64 characters before it's written or shown; it's written by temp name and rename in the checked sidecar, and it's gone when the handle closes (tested with `open_exclusive("import")`).
- **`peek_dimensions`** reads only the header's width, which is in the clear in page 0 already.

after step 2 lands the OS keychain):
- **What's new:** "Keys without a passphrase: `mnemo init` makes a random
  key and keeps it in your OS keychain, so every tool opens the brain with
  nothing typed. Write down its recovery code (`mnemo recovery-code`, shown
  only to a person at a terminal) to open it on another machine. Scripts
  and CI pass the key in `MNEMO_KEY`, a key file or a key command."
- **Security section, the threat model:** "The keychain keeps the key out
  of config files, dotfile repositories, backups, screen shares and shell
  history, and away from other users of the machine. It doesn't keep it
  from programs running as you: any of them can read the keychain entry or
  run `mnemo recovery-code`. The recovery code is shown only to a person at
  a terminal, so it doesn't land in an agent's transcript by accident, but
  that isn't a barrier against a program that sets out to read it. 'The
  key no longer sits in plain text' is the whole claim."

no terminal). The CLI tests clear the markers and every `MNEMO_*`
variable from their children, so they behave the same under an agent,
in CI and in a person's terminal.

**One finding of mine, for step 2.** `resolve` calls `store.get(salt)?`
before it looks at any env source:
- A store error aborts the chain even when `MNEMO_KEY` is set.
- With the OS keychain, a lookup can raise a GUI prompt, or fail on a
  headless Linux machine with no Secret Service, when an earlier source
  would have answered.

Make the store lookup lazy:
- Query it only when no earlier source of the file's kind is present
  (it's the last in the chain), or for the one try of the other kind.
- A store error is a note when another source answers, and the error
  only when the store was the source chosen.
- Test: a store that errors, with `MNEMO_KEY` set, opens through
  `MNEMO_KEY` with a note.

- One docs commit, a new section "LOCK-2: the writer safety valve
  (v0.15.0 step 2b; design for review)", after "Writer preference, then
  readers first".
- CI 14/14. No code, no format change.

**What the section decides, against your seven points:**
1. **The shape:**
   - A writer that has waited T tries `writer.lock` exclusively on every
     retry until it holds it, then goes on through the intent and main
     locks, and releases the valve as soon as it holds the main lock.
   - Readers try the valve shared without waiting before the intent lock,
     and back off while it's held.
   - It names why the writer can get the valve when it couldn't get the
     intent lock: a reader holds it for about 2 µs (two system calls)
     against tens of µs for the intent lock.
   - It says how it differs from step 5's newcomer rule (only writers
     hold it, and only after T), and why readers can't starve (two
     writers, a dead writer, a stopped writer, a compaction past T).
   - **A fallback is noted,** not planned: a one-byte flag that readers
     `pread`, locking the valve only when it's set, if the bench shows
     writers still can't get the valve.
2. **The file: a new `writer.lock` in the existing sidecar directory, not
   a byte range in `intent.lock`.**
   - `fs4` has whole-file locks only (`flock`; `LockFileEx` from 0 for
     the full length).
   - Unix ranges would need `fcntl` locks, which drop when the process
     closes any descriptor of the file (two handles in one process), and
     interact with `flock` on macOS.
   - A Windows range would need `unsafe` FFI, which the crate forbids.
   - The file: created by the first writer past T (`O_EXCL`,
     `O_NOFOLLOW`, close-on-exec, 0600) or up front by a v0.15 sidecar;
     never by a reader. A read-only directory means no valve and the
     existing notice. No cleanup. No new sibling of the brain.
3. **The platforms:** `flock` through fs4 on macOS and Linux, and
   `LockFileEx` with `FAIL_IMMEDIATELY` on Windows. The reader's try is
   non-blocking. NFS and SMB: unchanged.
4. **Old builds:** a v0.14 reader skips the valve, so against v0.14 readers
   a v0.15 writer is only as bounded as today. Nothing breaks. The docs
   line: "the bound holds when every process using the file shared runs
   v0.15 or later".
5. **`for_plain`:** in `acquire`, before each wait, one `lstat` for the
   sidecar. It's opened with every check once it appears, and never
   created.
6. **The bench and tests:**
   - **Machine:** the Apple M1 Pro, as step 5.
   - **Cells:** the cheap-read cells at 8 and 16 readers (target no
     `Locked`); readers alone; step 5's six mixes against
     `shared_v0_14_0`; a T sweep.
   - **Eight tests:** the 1 s bound; 16 cheap readers; the valve held only
     past T; a writer killed holding the valve; two writers; `for_plain`;
     no valve available; a missing `writer.lock`.
7. **What it costs a reader:** about 2 µs a window with the descriptor
   kept (about 3 µs while `writer.lock` doesn't exist yet). That's about
   2 percent of a cheap `get` and well under 1 percent of a recall, to be
   measured.

**A decision for you: T against the 1 s bound.** They conflict as written.
- A writer that takes the valve only after about 2 s can wait more than

  largest T that keeps the 1 s bound and "no `Locked`" at 8 and 16
  readers, provided readers' p99 in the 1-writer, 7-reader mix stays
  within about one commit (50 ms).
- **The alternative:** keep about 2 s, and make the test's bound about
  2.5 s.

### 2026-11-14 — WORKER — DONE — LOCK-2 round 2: the writer safety valve's code, T = 500 ms (PR 80, `48471b8`); green, not merged

Per the REVIEW + DECISION + DISPATCH "LOCK-2's paper accepted; T = 500 ms
by the sweep rule; the code (round 2 of 3)".

**PR 80** (`rel0150-2b-lock2` → `release-0.15.0`):
- The paper commit plus `48471b8`.
- CI 43589143670: 14/14. The restored 1 s writer bound held on the macOS,

  - `cargo test --features failpoints`: **520 passed, 0 failed**;
  - uniffi 21 passed, 1 ignored;
  - fmt and clippy are clean (with and without `keychain`);
  - the `cargo +1.75 --locked` build passes.
- No format change, no new dependency.

**What it builds** (the section as written, plus one rule from the
bench):
- **The valve:** `writer.lock` in the sidecar.
  - A writer that has waited T (500 ms; `MNEMO_DEV_VALVE_MS` in dev-hooks)
    tries it exclusively before each backoff, until it holds it. It
    releases the valve when it gets the main lock, before the intent lock.
  - **Retries past T:** 1 to 2 ms jittered (`Call::hurry`), from the
    moment the writer passes T.
- **Readers:** a shared try without waiting, then the unlock, before the
  intent lock, on a descriptor the sidecar keeps once the file exists
  (`Sidecar::valve_for_reading`). A conflict means back off.
- **The file:** a v0.15 shared handle's sidecar makes it up front. A writer
  past T makes it if it's missing (a pre-v0.15 sidecar). A reader never
  does.
- **If the valve can't be taken:** the sidecar is reopened by path once
  per call, as the intent lock does (RB-007.7).
  - When the valve still can't be made or opened, the write goes on
    without it, and a notice is given once.
  - Not for `NotFound`, which is a directory being removed; the existing
    "sidecar removed while two processes write" test asserts no notices.
- **`for_plain`:** an `lstat` before each wait; once the sidecar appears,
  it's opened with every check, and never created.
- **The bench's baseline:** `MNEMO_DEV_NO_VALVE` (dev-hooks only) turns
  the valve off.

**A change from the paper (for your review): a reader that has itself
waited T stops deferring to the valve.**
- The first bench run, with the rule as written, starved readers in step
  5's 8-writer, 2-reader mix: 2.5 reads a second, p99 3.4 s. Most writers'
  calls pass T there, so the valve went from writer to writer with hardly
  a gap. The paper's "about (writers past T) × one commit" was wrong for a
  saturating mix.
- With the reader rule, those readers get 71 reads a second, p99 about
  1.06 s.
- Cheap readers never reach T, so the lockout fix is untouched.

from other sessions, so noisier than `shared_v0_14_0`;

| 2000 ms | bench writer p99 2053 ms: **over** | 0 / 0 | 0.53 ms | 2036 / 2069 ms |

**The client table** (each path and format fetched 2026-11-14 from the
vendor's docs and cited in `src/bin/mnemo/mcp_install.rs`):

| Client | Scopes | Where | Project path |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude-code` | project, local, user | `claude mcp add-json <name> '<json>' --scope …` when `claude` is on the PATH (run in the project root); otherwise `.mcp.json` at the project root, project only (local and user live in `~/.claude.json`, which only `claude` writes) | `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/<path>`: the docs say Claude Code sets `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` in the server's environment and `.mcp.json` expands `${VAR:-default}` in `args` |
| `cursor` | project, user | `.cursor/mcp.json`, `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | `${workspaceFolder}/<path>` (documented) |
| `claude-desktop` | user | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/` (macOS), `%APPDATA%\Claude\` (Windows), `~/.config/Claude/` (Linux), `claude_desktop_config.json` | n/a; its docs ask for absolute paths |

**Left out, as allowed:**
- **VS Code:** it has two formats now. Its portable project file is the
  same `.mcp.json` at the root that Claude Code reads, and the two clients
  expand different variables (`${workspaceFolder}` against
  `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`). So it isn't "just a table entry".
- **Codex:** TOML, which would need a TOML-editing dependency.

**The decisions:**
- **The working directory:** none of the three documents what directory a
  project server starts in. So a project path uses each client's
  documented variable rather than relying on the working directory.
- **The command:** `mnemo` from the PATH in a project scope. In the user
  and local scopes, the absolute path of the running `mnemo` (a GUI client
  like Claude Desktop doesn't get the shell's PATH), with the brain's path
  absolute too.
- **The rules,** checked in code before anything is written: always
  `--shared`, no `env` in the entry, and no absolute path, `--embed-cmd`
  or key command in a project scope.
- **The default scope:** `project` when the brain is inside the current
  git work tree (found by walking up for `.git`, no `git` binary) and the
  client has a project scope; `user` otherwise. A scope a client doesn't
  have is an error naming the ones it has.
- **The write:**
  - an order-keeping merge, so other servers' and keys' text is kept byte
    for byte. That's serde_json's `raw_value` feature, which adds no
    crate;
  - an existing entry with the same name is replaced after the diff and a
    confirm (or `--yes`);
  - an atomic temp-and-rename that keeps the file's mode;
  - a parse error stops it, with nothing written.
- **The diff:** a line diff of the masked, pretty old and new configs
  (every `env` and `headers` value masked). With `claude`, it's the JSON
  passed to `add-json`. If `add-json` fails because the name exists, the
  message names `claude mcp remove`.
- **A passphrase:**
  - **A passphrase brain:** "the server will need MNEMO_PASSPHRASE … or
    the passphrase in the keychain". A key brain not in the keychain is
    pointed at `mnemo unlock`.
  - **A `MNEMO_PASSPHRASE` in the entry being replaced:** at a terminal,
    it offers to move it into the keychain, checking it opens the brain
    first.
  - `--yes` never moves it: it stops, with nothing written, rather than
    drop a working passphrase silently. The passphrase is never printed.
- **Not at a terminal without `--yes`:** nothing is written, and the
  message says so.

**Tests** (`tests/mcp_install_cli.rs`, 10, plus 2 unit tests). Every run
uses a temporary `HOME`, `APPDATA` and `PATH` (with at most a fake
`claude` that records its arguments) and `MNEMO_DEV_NO_KEYCHAIN`. Nothing
ran against this Mac's client configs or the real `claude`.
- cursor project (relative, the three rules) and user (absolute);
- claude-code without `claude` (`.mcp.json` with the project variable;

- claude-desktop (the user scope by default inside a repository; project

- the merge keeping another server's exact text and a top-level key;
- the parse-error stop;
- `--print` writing nothing, and `env` masking;
- `--yes` refusing to drop a `MNEMO_PASSPHRASE`;
- no terminal means no write, then a replace with `--yes`;
- a project scope refusing a brain outside the project;
- the key-brain note.

**My reading of the cause** (by reading the code, not yet measured):
- A reader past T stops deferring to the valve, but then queues on the
  intent lock with its normal doubling backoff, up to 50 ms between tries.
- The eight writers past T retry every 1 to 2 ms (`Call::hurry`), and each
  holds the intent lock exclusively while it waits for the main lock.
- `flock` has no queue, so a reader trying every 50 ms almost never finds
  the gap between one hurried writer's release and the next one's take.
- The faster machine leaves more gaps.

**A proposed fix** (LOCK-2 code; not done, since it's LOCK-2's last round
before you take it to the user):
- **A reader past T hurries too** (1 to 2 ms retries), so it competes on
  equal terms. Optionally, it also keeps the intent lock shared once it
  holds it, as a reader waiting for a writer already does.
- **The check:** the eight-writer test on CI and locally, and step 5's
  8w+2r and 4w+2r cells, against today's numbers.
- **The alternative,** if you'd rather not touch LOCK-2 again before the
  user: mark that test `#[ignore]` with a note, and state in the docs that
  readers can starve with eight writers looping on a slow machine.

### 2026-11-14 — PLANNER-A — DECISION + DISPATCH — the user ships LOCK-2 as it is, and "reads never wait for saves" is planned for later; merge PRs 82 and 81; step 4's code: retrieval

**The user's decision (2026-11-14):** "Ship it, plan reads-never-wait
later."
- LOCK-2 stays as round 3 built it.
- The eight-writer test asserts what's guaranteed, not a read count.
- The user asked why readers need managing at all. I explained in
  `planner-a`:
  - one file, and a save rewrites part of it, so reads and saves take
    turns;
  - v0.14's readers-first locked saves out;
  - LOCK-2 is SQLite's classic "pending" lock.
  - **The long-term answer** is how SQLite's WAL mode, Postgres and LMDB
    work: readers keep reading the last committed state while a save is
    written, so they never wait for one.

**Carried as SNAP-1, "reads never wait for saves"** (the user schedules
it; not v0.15):
- Readers read the last committed snapshot while a writer commits, so
  only writers wait for writers.
- It starts with a design note: what a commit rewrites in place today,
  whether the WAL can serve readers, and whether it needs a format
  version.
- I'll put it in front of the user at the next roadmap choice, with
  PERF-2 and background saves, which it overlaps.

**PR 83, test-only, not dispatched (yours to accept):**
- `a_plain_operation_picks_up_the_sidecar_while_it_waits` (PR 80's) failed
  2 of 14 local runs at load averages of 17 to 35, with "it didn't pick up
  the sidecar".
- **The cause is the test's setup.** It gave sixteen readers 100 ms to
  start. If they left a gap, the plain operation got in at once, and an
  operation that never waits never looks for the sidecar.
- **The fix:** wait for the readers' first read, then hold a shared lock
  for 300 ms as the operation starts. It now always waits (510 to 540 ms,
  through the valve). It passed 13 of 13 local runs, and CI 43608179050
  was 14/14.
- Head `cb685c0`, into `release-0.15.0`. No engine code changes. I haven't
  merged it.

**Step 4: BLOCKED before any code, on TOK-1's "recorded in the BM25
manifest, with no format change".**
- **The evidence.** `load_bm25_manifest` (`mnemo/src/store/records.rs`,
  line 359) refuses any `tokenizer` other than 1: "BM25 tokenizer {} is
  newer than this build understands". It runs on every open
  (`open.rs`: `let bm25_manifest = load_bm25_manifest(&mut pager,
  header.bm25)?;`). The released code has the same check and call:
  `git show v0.14.0:mnemo/src/store/records.rs` line 361 and `open.rs`
  line 803, and v0.12.3's `records.rs` line 353.
- **So:** a file whose manifest says tokenizer 2 can't be opened by v0.12
  to v0.14 at all, read-only included. Under the spec, that's every file
  v0.15 creates and every file it compacts or re-embeds. That includes an
  app on v0.14 handed such a file. The format version doesn't move, but for
  older builds the effect is a format break.
- **The options** (detailed in the draft note's section 3):
  1. **The manifest byte, as specified.** It's simple, and nothing mixes
     tokenizers. Older builds are refused with that message.
  2. **A reserved `_mnemo.bm25` cache entry** (JSON) holding the tokenizer,
     with the manifest byte left at 1. Older builds keep opening and
     querying the file, since tokenizer 2 indexes every tokenizer 1 token.
     **The cost:** documents an older build writes get tokenizer 1 tokens
     only, so parts don't match them until the next v0.15 compaction. An
     older build's compaction leaves a tokenizer 1 index under an entry
     that says 2: whole tokens match, parts find nothing until v0.15
     compacts it.
  3. **Defer TOK-1** to the next format version, and document that keywords
     match whole words as written.
- **My recommendation is 2.** The file stays usable by every v9 build. The
  degraded case needs an older build writing to a v0.15 file, which the
  shared-mode guide already says to avoid. If it's 1, I'd add a CHANGELOG
  line that v0.15 files need v0.15 to open.

**The rest of step 4 is designed, not coded.** The draft is
`docs/design/12.3-retrieval.md`, untracked; it goes into step 4's PR. Your
points, settled:
- **`embed_query`** defaults to `embed`.
  - Only recalls by text use it: `from_text`, the CLI's `recall --text`,
    the MCP `recall` (and its pre-embed), and Python's `recall_text`.
  - Semantic-cache text keeps `embed` on both sides.
  - `EmbedderIdentity` gains `query_convention: String`. It's empty for
    symmetric embedders, and written to the two JSON identities only when
    non-empty, so existing files are unchanged.
  - It derives `Default`. The new field is a breaking change for
    hand-built literals (CHANGELOG Changed).
  - Older builds ignore the field.
- **`--embed-cmd`:** a new flag, `--embed-query <convention>`, makes each
  request a JSON object, `{"kind":"query"|"document","text":…}`. Without
  it the protocol is unchanged. Not an environment variable: one child
  serves both sides for a handle's whole life.
- **Python:** `set_embedder(…, query_fn=None, query_convention=None)`.
  Both or neither, or a `ValueError`. One-argument callables are
  unchanged.
- **Mobile:** unchanged. An asymmetric file is refused there by the
  mismatch check.
- **Hybrid by default:** `RecallRequest.text`, set by `from_text`, is used
  for BM25 when `keywords` is `None`. Explicit keywords replace it.
  - It's ignored on v8, rather than failing as explicit keywords do there.
  - **The opt-out is empty keywords** on every surface, plus `--no-keywords`
    in the CLI.
  - The weight is the same ε = 0.5, pending the measurements.
- **`reembed`:**
  - It's compaction with new vectors: under the exclusive lock, which it
    waits for as compaction does (`--wait`), into a temp file with the
    salt kept, then renamed under the lock.
  - It re-embeds every live memory (document side, batches of 64) except
    the manifest's sentinel.
  - It records the new identity in both places. The width may change.
  - The CLI flags are the existing `--embed-cmd`/`--embed-name` plus
    `--embed-query`. Step 5 adds the built-in one.
- **Which operations rebuild BM25:** compaction and `reembed`, both since
  they write a new file. Under option 1 or 2, new files start at
  tokenizer 2.

     file as mixed:

       has them;

1. **Where tokenizer 2 is recorded: a mark in each keyword segment,** not
   the manifest memory or a cache entry.

     the reserved term `"\0mnemo.tokenizer.2"`, posting document 0. A v0.15
     merge of mixed segments carries `"\0mnemo.tokenizer.mixed"`.
   - **Why not the manifest:** only `mnemo init` writes one, so files made
     with `Mnemo::create`, Python's `open` or the mobile binding have none.
     And either your location or a cache entry would need the stamp
     rewritten on every commit that indexes a document.
   - **The mark is its own staleness stamp, at no extra write.** Older
     builds leave existing segments as they are. What they add has no
     mark:
     - their writes add unmarked segments;
     - their merges drop the mark (its only posting, document 0, is never
       live);
     - their compaction rebuilds the index unmarked.
   - **State:**
     - no segments, or all marked 2: tokenizer 2;
     - none marked: tokenizer 1, and v0.15 keeps it pure;
     - otherwise mixed.
   - **A mixed index is queried with tokenizer 2:** whole tokens match
     every document; parts match the tokenizer 2 ones. It stays mixed until
     a v0.15 compaction or `reembed`.

  never sets `keyring-core`'s process-wide default store.

    (service, account).

    same little-endian UTF-16 password.
  - **Linux:** 3.6.3 tags `service`, `username`, `target` and
    `application`; 4.x searches by `service` and `username`, so it finds
    them.

    keychain.

Brain: "which embedding model is the built-in default and why" → hit
(rank 1, sim 0.41), the Worker's comparison fact. Tally: 6 lookups, 3
hits, 1 partial, 2 misses (not stored).

**Checked:**

  `rel0150-5-embedder` only) exist, and CI 43630828497 passed.

- **`ort-sys` 2.0.0-rc.15's `dist.tsv`:**
  - it has no `x86_64-apple-darwin` row;
  - Windows x86_64 has no CPU-only build (its smallest is `directml`);
  - every binary comes from `cdn.pyke.io`, a third party's CDN, fetched
    at build time. That's a supply-chain input to the release builds
    that step 5's spec didn't name.

**My reading:**
- **The model is the easy call: `snowflake-arctic-embed-xs`.**
  - It's the best vector-only (29/30, MRR 0.983), the fastest (0.64 s
    cold, 24 ms a memory) and the smallest (91 MB). It's Apache-2.0, and
    it has first-party ONNX and safetensors weights.
  - It "wins clearly" on speed and size, and is level or better on
    quality, so the spec's bge-small default gives way.
  - The 0.25 keyword weight gets re-set for it (q01 and q15).
- **The runtime is the real question.** ONNX Runtime through `fastembed`:
  - is over the 30 MB budget unstripped on macOS arm64, and likely on
    Windows;
  - has no Intel Mac build;
  - needs clang's runtime to link on macOS;
  - downloads its binary from a third-party CDN at build time;
  - and none of it is usable on the phones this phase.
- **A pure-Rust runtime** (`candle`'s BERT, or `tract` for ONNX) would
  run the same BERT-family model on every target, Intel Mac included,
  with no C++ library and no build-time download. Its size and speed are
  unmeasured. The tokenizer crate's size counts against either runtime.

**The user decides:**
- the model;
- the runtime:
  - **(a)** measure a pure-Rust runtime with arctic-xs first;
  - **(b)** ship ONNX Runtime now, with stripped binaries and keyword-only
    recall on the targets it can't serve;
  - **(c)** take the built-in embedder out of v0.15.

  --offline --release --features embed-candle --example candle_size`
  builds. Nothing in candle downloads (unlike `ort-sys`).
- **No new C or C++:** with `embed-candle` on, the only crate that builds
  with `cc` is still `zstd-sys` (`cargo tree -i cc`, on macOS and Linux).
  `esaxx-rs` is in the graph, but without its C++ feature.
- **`cargo deny` with `keychain,embed-candle`:** advisories, bans and
  sources OK; licences FAILED on one, **Zlib** (`foldhash` 0.2.0, through
  `hashbrown` 0.16 and `safetensors` 0.8). Its 23 duplicate warnings
  include **9 new:** `fancy-regex`, `hashbrown`, `r-efi`, `rand`,
  `rand_chacha`, `rand_core`, `strsim`, `thiserror` and `thiserror-impl`.
  I added no exceptions.

**6. Against part 1's ONNX Runtime:**

| | candle (pure Rust) | ONNX Runtime (fastembed) |
|---|---|---|
| Growth, macOS arm64 | +4.5 MiB as built, +4.1 MiB stripped | +32.7 MB as built, +24.0 MB stripped |
| Over 30 MB? | **no, on all four** | **yes as built** on macOS arm64; likely Linux; likely Windows (DirectML is 3.4× the download) |
| Cold `remember` (arctic-xs) | 86 ms | 636 ms |
| Per memory (arctic-xs) | 22.5 ms | 24.2 ms |
| Peak RSS | 207 MB one `remember`, 0.8 GB re-embed | 4.1 GB (the comparison process) |
| Targets | macOS arm64 and x86_64, Linux x86_64 and aarch64; iOS and Android build | no x86_64 macOS build; macOS needs clang's runtime linked |
| Build-time inputs | crates only | `ort-sys` downloads a prebuilt ONNX Runtime (9.7 to 32.5 MB) at build time |
| New C/C++ | none | the prebuilt C++ library |
| `cargo deny` | 1 licence (Zlib), 9 new duplicates | 7 licences |

**My reading:**

  needed.

1. **The extraction rule, fixed here.** Put it in a function in the
   harness, and commit it, with its unit cases, before any run. A token
   is the query split on whitespace, with these stripped from each end:
   ``` ` ' " , . ; : ? ! ( ) [ ] { } ```.
   - **It's an identifier if** it was inside backticks in the query, or
     any of these holds:
     - it contains `::`, `@` or `=`;
     - it starts with `--`;
     - it contains `_` between two letters or digits;
     - it is camelCase or PascalCase with an inner capital, matching
       `[a-z][A-Z]` or `[A-Z][a-z]+[A-Z]`;
     - it is a `name(…)` call, with `(` after a letter, kept before
       stripping;
     - it is a dotted name, matching `[A-Za-z_]+\.[A-Za-z_]+`, which also
       takes `store.rs`.
   - **Not identifiers:** plain words, numbers and versions like `1.92`.
   - **Then:** no identifier found means vector-only (text weight 0). If
     identifiers are found, they're passed as explicit keywords at the
     engine's explicit weight, 0.5, and the plain words still get 0. An
     explicit `keywords` from the caller overrides the rule, as now.
   - **Unit cases**, with what each should extract:
     - "what does `snapshot_list` return" → `snapshot_list`;
     - "why use --features failpoints,benches,keychain" → `--features`
       and `failpoints,benches,keychain`, since `--` starts the first.
       The second is a plain token, but add it if it follows a `--` flag.
     - "RecallRequest::from_text defaults" → `RecallRequest::from_text`;
     - "where does keyring@3.6.3 store it" → `keyring@3.6.3`;
     - "why 1.92" → nothing;
     - "who is the product for" → nothing.

**Step 5b: supersede a named memory.** Branch `rel0150-5b-supersede`
from `release-0.15.0`, with a PR into it. It is ACTIVE now; part 4
follows it.

1. **The semantics: adopt, then supersede, through the existing keyed
   path.**
   - A keyed write naming one existing memory id writes the old record
     into the key's slot as its predecessor:
     - the new record gets `_mnemo.supersedes = <old id>`;
     - the old one gets `_mnemo.key = <key>`, `_mnemo.superseded_by` and
       `_mnemo.invalid_at`.
   - Then `history(key)` lists it as the oldest version, with no change
     to `history_in`. Recall and `about` exclude it, as for any
     superseded record.
   - **One id per call.** `_mnemo.supersedes` stays a single string, so
     nothing about an existing record's shape changes, and older builds
     carry it through as `_mnemo.*` metadata. **No format change.**
   - If the new content matches the old record's user-visible fields,
     the outcome follows the existing identical-write rule. Say what you
     chose, and test it.
2. **The refusals**, each an `Invalid` with a clear message and a test:
   - the id doesn't exist, or is deleted;
   - it's already superseded;
   - it already carries a `_mnemo.key` (use the plain keyed write);
   - the key's slot already has a live record (one predecessor only);
   - it's an engine record (any `_mnemo.kind`: threads, essence, the
     manifest);
   - it's a Private memory of another agent, or the scopes don't match
     the slot's (Private for this agent, or Shared);
   - the handle is read-only.
3. **The caches and reopen:**
   - the slot index and the superseded set are updated as in
     `remember_keyed`;
   - **after reopen,** the cache rebuild (`ensure_key_caches`) must treat
     the adopted record as superseded, never as the slot's live record,
     although it now carries `_mnemo.key`;
   - test it across a reopen and across a compaction;
   - shared mode writes it under the writer lock, like any mutating call.
4. **The surfaces:**
   - Rust: a new method or an options form of `remember_keyed`, following
     the module's naming. Name it in the DONE.
   - Python: `supersedes=` beside `key=`.
   - CLI: `mnemo remember --key K --supersedes <id>`.
   - MCP: a `supersedes` argument on the keyed remember tool.
   - `test/scripts/project_memory.py`: `remember --key K --supersedes
     <id>`.
   - Not UniFFI this phase; carried.
5. **Compat:** the `compat (v0.14.0, linux)` job, or a test like it,
   opens a file holding an adopted record with v0.14.0. The record is
   excluded from recall, and its history reads.
6. **Docs:** the crate README (the keyed-write section), the Python

**The method: `Mnemo::remember_keyed_superseding(memory, key, &old_id)
-> (Ulid, WriteOutcome)`,** plus `remember_keyed_text_superseding` (the
embedder's document side). It's a sibling of `remember_keyed`, following
the module's naming.
- **It adopts, then supersedes:**
  - the old record takes `_mnemo.key` and is marked
    `_mnemo.superseded_by` and `_mnemo.invalid_at`;
  - the new one gets `_mnemo.supersedes = <old>`;
  - the caches are updated as in `remember_keyed`.
  - `history(key)` lists the old record as the oldest version.
    `history_in` is unchanged.
- **Identical content (my choice):** no new record. The old record takes
  the key and becomes the slot's **live** record, and the outcome is
  **`Updated`** with the old id. `Unchanged` would claim "no record was
  written", which is false here: the old record gains its key. Tested.
- **The refusals,** each `Invalid` with a message and a test, plus
  `ReadOnly`:
  - no such memory;
  - deleted;
  - already superseded;
  - already has a key ("use the plain keyed write");
  - the key's slot already has a live record;
  - an engine record (any `_mnemo.kind`, or the manifest by its topic,
    since the scaffold manifest has no kind);
  - not in the slot's scope: another agent's Private memory, or Shared
    against Private. A Shared write takes a Shared memory; tested;
  - an empty key, or `_mnemo.*` metadata from the caller.
- **The caches needed no change.** `ensure_key_caches` puts a record with
  `_mnemo.superseded_by` into the superseded set **before** it reads its
  key (`crud.rs`), so an adopted record is never taken as the slot's live
  record.
  - Tested across a reopen and across a compaction: the history,
    recall's exclusion, and an identical keyed write afterwards returning
    `Unchanged` with the new record's id.
  - Shared mode writes it in a write window, under the writer lock;
    tested.
- **No format change:** the keyed path's own `_mnemo.*` keys, with
  `_mnemo.supersedes` still one string.

**The surfaces:**
- the CLI: `mnemo remember --key K --supersedes <ID>` (`requires = "key"`;
  prints `id\tsuperseded`, or `updated`);
- Python: `supersedes=` on `remember` and `remember_text` (a `ValueError`
  without `key=`);
- MCP: `supersedes` on `remember` (it needs `key`);

  1.100 pass.**

    features, and give `embed-candle` its own floor of 1.94: the MSRV jobs
    build without it at 1.92, plus one 1.94 build with it. The release
    builds use stable, so they're unaffected. Step 5a's finding (Cargo

- **1w+1r stays above 5 ms. The explanation, with a check:**
  - **The worst read matches one write in every run:** 129 to 158 ms,
    against the writer's 131 to 142 ms. So each commit makes about one
    read wait for it.
  - **The p99 lands on those waits whenever the reader does fewer than
    about 100 reads per write.** Writes over reads were 3.0%, 2.1% and 1.9%
    in the three runs.
  - **The check:** the same cell run back to back, with the valve and with
    `MNEMO_DEV_NO_VALVE`. With the valve: read p99 0.29 ms over 14,513
    reads (0.9% coincide). Without it: 38 ms over 11,198 reads (1.2%). The
    worst read was 157 and 146 ms.
  - **So the valve isn't the cause.** The reader's rate decides the number,
    and it swings threefold with machine load. That fits v0.14's 0.11 ms,
    if that run's reader was fast.
  - **For a stable figure:** p99.9, or the wait per commit, rather than
    p99. I haven't changed the bench.
